span.subject: Binary search
span.text: In computer science, binary search, also known as half-interval search,[1] logarithmic search,[2] or binary chop,[3] is a search algorithm that finds the position of a target value within a sorted array.[4][5] Binary search compares the target value to the middle element of the array.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Compost is a mixture of ingredients used as plant fertilizer and to improve soil's physical, chemical, and biological properties.

references.label: P1.1
references.text: Compost is a mixture of ingredients used as plant fertilizer and to improve soil's physical, chemical, and biological properties.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: It is commonly prepared by decomposing plant and food waste, recycling organic materials, and manure.

references.label: P1.2
references.text: It is commonly prepared by decomposing plant and food waste, recycling organic materials, and manure.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: The resulting mixture is rich in plant nutrients and beneficial organisms, such as bacteria, protozoa, nematodes, and fungi.

references.label: P1.3
references.text: The resulting mixture is rich in plant nutrients and beneficial organisms, such as bacteria, protozoa, nematodes, and fungi.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Compost improves soil fertility in gardens, landscaping, horticulture, urban agriculture, and organic farming, reducing dependency on commercial chemical fertilizers.[1] The benefits of compost include providing nutrients to crops as fertilizer, acting as a soil conditioner, increasing the humus or humic acid contents of the soil, and introducing beneficial microbes that help to suppress pathogens in the soil and reduce soil-borne diseases.

references.label: P1.4
references.text: Compost improves soil fertility in gardens, landscaping, horticulture, urban agriculture, and organic farming, reducing dependency on commercial chemical fertilizers.[1] The benefits of compost include providing nutrients to crops as fertilizer, acting as a soil conditioner, increasing the humus or humic acid contents of the soil, and introducing beneficial microbes that help to suppress pathogens in the soil and reduce soil-borne diseases.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: At the most basic level, composting requires gathering a mix of green waste (nitrogen-rich materials such as leaves, grass, and food scraps) and brown waste (woody materials rich in carbon, such as stalks, paper, and wood chips).[1] The materials break down into humus in a process taking months.[2] Composting can be a multistep, closely monitored process with measured inputs of water, air, and carbon- and nitrogen-rich materials.

references.label: P2.1
references.text: At the most basic level, composting requires gathering a mix of green waste (nitrogen-rich materials such as leaves, grass, and food scraps) and brown waste (woody materials rich in carbon, such as stalks, paper, and wood chips).[1] The materials break down into humus in a process taking months.[2] Composting can be a multistep, closely monitored process with measured inputs of water, air, and carbon- and nitrogen-rich materials.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: The decomposition process is aided by shredding the plant matter, adding water, and ensuring proper aeration by regularly turning the mixture in a process using open piles or windrows.[1][3] Fungi, earthworms, and other detritivores further break up the organic material.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Aerobic bacteria and fungi manage the chemical process by converting the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide, and ammonium ions.

references.label: P2.3
references.text: Aerobic bacteria and fungi manage the chemical process by converting the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide, and ammonium ions.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Composting is an important part of waste management, since food and other compostable materials make up about 20% of waste in landfills, and due to anaerobic conditions, these materials take longer to biodegrade in the landfill.[4][5] Composting offers an environmentally superior alternative to using organic material for landfill because composting reduces methane emissions due to anaerobic conditions, and provides economic and environmental co-benefits.[6][7] For example, compost can also be used for land and stream reclamation, wetland construction, and landfill cover.

span.subject: Vermicompost
span.text: Vermicompost (vermi-compost) is the product of the decomposition process using various species of worms, usually red wigglers, white worms, and other earthworms, to create a mixture of decomposing vegetable or food waste, bedding materials, and vermicast.

span.subject: Vermicompost
span.text: Vermicast (also called worm castings,[a] worm humus, worm poop, worm manure, or worm faeces) is the end-product of the breakdown of organic matter by earthworms.[1] These excreta have been shown to contain reduced levels of contaminants and a higher saturation of nutrients than the organic materials before vermicomposting.[2]

span.subject: Constitutional monarchy
span.text: In countries such as Liechtenstein, Monaco, Morocco, Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain, Thailand and Bhutan, the constitution grants substantial discretionary powers to the sovereign, while in United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms, the Netherlands, Spain, Luxembourg, Belgium, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Lesotho, Malaysia, Cambodia, and Japan, the monarch retains significantly less, if any, personal discretion in the exercise of their authority.

span.subject: Aruba

span.subject: Fermentation
span.text: Fermentation is a type of anaerobic metabolism that harnesses the redox potential of the reactants to make adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and organic end products.[1][2] Organic molecules, such as glucose or other sugars, are catabolized and their electrons are transferred to other organic molecules (cofactors, coenzymes, etc.).[1] Anaerobic glycolysis is a related term used to describe the occurrence of fermentation in organisms (usually multicellular organisms such as animals) when aerobic respiration cannot keep up with the ATP demand, due to insufficient oxygen supply or anaerobic conditions.

span.subject: Apparent magnitude
span.text: Apparent magnitude (m) is a measure of the brightness of a star, astronomical object or other celestial objects like artificial satellites.

references.label: P4.1
references.text: Apparent magnitude (m) is a measure of the brightness of a star, astronomical object or other celestial objects like artificial satellites.

span.subject: Apparent magnitude
span.text: Its value depends on its intrinsic luminosity, its distance, and any extinction of the object's light caused by interstellar dust or atmosphere along the line of sight to the observer.

references.label: P4.2
references.text: Its value depends on its intrinsic luminosity, its distance, and any extinction of the object's light caused by interstellar dust or atmosphere along the line of sight to the observer.

span.subject: Apparent magnitude
span.text: The scale is reverse logarithmic: the brighter an object is, the lower its magnitude number.

references.label: P5.1
references.text: The scale is reverse logarithmic: the brighter an object is, the lower its magnitude number.

span.subject: Apparent magnitude
span.text: A difference of 1.0 in magnitude corresponds to the brightness ratio of [TeX: {\displaystyle {\sqrt[{5}]{100}}}] , or about 2.512.

references.label: P5.2

span.subject: Apparent magnitude
span.text: For example, a magnitude 2.0 star is 2.512 times as bright as a magnitude 3.0 star, 6.31 times as bright as a magnitude 4.0 star, and precisely 100 times as bright as a magnitude 7.0 star.

span.text: The brightest astronomical objects have negative apparent magnitudes, such as Venus at magnitude −4.2 or Sirius at magnitude −1.46.

span.subject: Apparent magnitude
span.text: The faintest stars visible with the naked eye on the darkest night have apparent magnitudes of about +6.5, though this varies depending on a person's eyesight, their altitude, and atmospheric conditions when viewing.[2] The apparent magnitude of known objects can range from −26.832 for our Sun to about +31.5 for objects in deep space imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope.[3]

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Compost is a mixture of ingredients used as plant fertilizer and to improve soil's physical, chemical, and biological properties.

references.label: P1.1
references.text: Compost is a mixture of ingredients used as plant fertilizer and to improve soil's physical, chemical, and biological properties.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: It is commonly prepared by decomposing plant and food waste, recycling organic materials, and manure.

references.label: P1.2
references.text: It is commonly prepared by decomposing plant and food waste, recycling organic materials, and manure.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: The resulting mixture is rich in plant nutrients and beneficial organisms, such as bacteria, protozoa, nematodes, and fungi.

references.label: P1.3
references.text: The resulting mixture is rich in plant nutrients and beneficial organisms, such as bacteria, protozoa, nematodes, and fungi.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Compost improves soil fertility in gardens, landscaping, horticulture, urban agriculture, and organic farming, reducing dependency on commercial chemical fertilizers.[1] The benefits of compost include providing nutrients to crops as fertilizer, acting as a soil conditioner, increasing the humus or humic acid contents of the soil, and introducing beneficial microbes that help to suppress pathogens in the soil and reduce soil-borne diseases.

references.label: P1.4
references.text: Compost improves soil fertility in gardens, landscaping, horticulture, urban agriculture, and organic farming, reducing dependency on commercial chemical fertilizers.[1] The benefits of compost include providing nutrients to crops as fertilizer, acting as a soil conditioner, increasing the humus or humic acid contents of the soil, and introducing beneficial microbes that help to suppress pathogens in the soil and reduce soil-borne diseases.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: At the most basic level, composting requires gathering a mix of green waste (nitrogen-rich materials such as leaves, grass, and food scraps) and brown waste (woody materials rich in carbon, such as stalks, paper, and wood chips).[1] The materials break down into humus in a process taking months.[2] Composting can be a multistep, closely monitored process with measured inputs of water, air, and carbon- and nitrogen-rich materials.

references.label: P2.1
references.text: At the most basic level, composting requires gathering a mix of green waste (nitrogen-rich materials such as leaves, grass, and food scraps) and brown waste (woody materials rich in carbon, such as stalks, paper, and wood chips).[1] The materials break down into humus in a process taking months.[2] Composting can be a multistep, closely monitored process with measured inputs of water, air, and carbon- and nitrogen-rich materials.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: The decomposition process is aided by shredding the plant matter, adding water, and ensuring proper aeration by regularly turning the mixture in a process using open piles or windrows.[1][3] Fungi, earthworms, and other detritivores further break up the organic material.

references.label: P2.2

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Aerobic bacteria and fungi manage the chemical process by converting the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide, and ammonium ions.

references.label: P2.3
references.text: Aerobic bacteria and fungi manage the chemical process by converting the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide, and ammonium ions.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Composting is an important part of waste management, since food and other compostable materials make up about 20% of waste in landfills, and due to anaerobic conditions, these materials take longer to biodegrade in the landfill.[4][5] Composting offers an environmentally superior alternative to using organic material for landfill because composting reduces methane emissions due to anaerobic conditions, and provides economic and environmental co-benefits.[6][7] For example, compost can also be used for land and stream reclamation, wetland construction, and landfill cover.

span.text: This process is called vermicomposting, with the rearing of worms for this purpose is called vermiculture.

span.subject: Vermicompost
span.text: Vermicast (also called worm castings,[a] worm humus, worm poop, worm manure, or worm faeces) is the end-product of the breakdown of organic matter by earthworms.[1] These excreta have been shown to contain reduced levels of contaminants and a higher saturation of nutrients than the organic materials before vermicomposting.[2]

span.text: Vermicompost contains water-soluble nutrients which may be extracted as vermiwash and is an excellent, nutrient-rich organic fertilizer and soil conditioner.[3] It is used in gardening and sustainable, organic farming.

span.subject: Constitution
span.text: A constitution, or supreme law, is the aggregate of fundamental principles or established precedents that constitute the legal basis of a polity, organization or other type of entity, and commonly determines how that entity is to be governed.[1]

span.subject: Constitution
span.text: When these principles are written down into a single document or set of legal documents, those documents may be said to embody a written constitution; if they are encompassed in a single comprehensive document, it is said to embody a codified constitution.

span.text: The constitution of the United Kingdom is a notable example of an uncodified constitution; it is instead written in numerous fundamental acts of a legislature, court cases, and treaties.[2]

span.subject: Constitutional monarchy
span.text: Constitutional monarchy, also known as limited monarchy, parliamentary monarchy or democratic monarchy, is a form of monarchy in which the monarch exercises their authority in accordance with a constitution and is not alone in making decisions.[1][2][3][4] Constitutional monarchies differ from absolute monarchies (in which a monarch is the only decision-maker) in that they are bound to exercise powers and authorities within limits prescribed by an established legal framework.

span.subject: Barcelona

span.subject: Fermentation
span.text: Fermentation is a type of anaerobic metabolism that harnesses the redox potential of the reactants to make adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and organic end products.[1][2] Organic molecules, such as glucose or other sugars, are catabolized and their electrons are transferred to other organic molecules (cofactors, coenzymes, etc.).[1] Anaerobic glycolysis is a related term used to describe the occurrence of fermentation in organisms (usually multicellular organisms such as animals) when aerobic respiration cannot keep up with the ATP demand, due to insufficient oxygen supply or anaerobic conditions.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Compost improves soil fertility in gardens, landscaping, horticulture, urban agriculture, and organic farming, reducing dependency on commercial chemical fertilizers.[1] The benefits of compost include providing nutrients to crops as fertilizer, acting as a soil conditioner, increasing the humus or humic acid contents of the soil, and introducing beneficial microbes that help to suppress pathogens in the soil and reduce soil-borne diseases.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: At the most basic level, composting requires gathering a mix of green waste (nitrogen-rich materials such as leaves, grass, and food scraps) and brown waste (woody materials rich in carbon, such as stalks, paper, and wood chips).[1] The materials break down into humus in a process taking months.[2] Composting can be a multistep, closely monitored process with measured inputs of water, air, and carbon- and nitrogen-rich materials.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: The decomposition process is aided by shredding the plant matter, adding water, and ensuring proper aeration by regularly turning the mixture in a process using open piles or windrows.[1][3] Fungi, earthworms, and other detritivores further break up the organic material.

span.text: Aerobic bacteria and fungi manage the chemical process by converting the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide, and ammonium ions.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Composting is an important part of waste management, since food and other compostable materials make up about 20% of waste in landfills, and due to anaerobic conditions, these materials take longer to biodegrade in the landfill.[4][5] Composting offers an environmentally superior alternative to using organic material for landfill because composting reduces methane emissions due to anaerobic conditions, and provides economic and environmental co-benefits.[6][7] For example, compost can also be used for land and stream reclamation, wetland construction, and landfill cover.

span.subject: Constitution
span.text: A constitution, or supreme law, is the aggregate of fundamental principles or established precedents that constitute the legal basis of a polity, organization or other type of entity, and commonly determines how that entity is to be governed.[1]

span.text: When these principles are written down into a single document or set of legal documents, those documents may be said to embody a written constitution; if they are encompassed in a single comprehensive document, it is said to embody a codified constitution.

span.subject: Constitutional monarchy
span.text: Constitutional monarchy, also known as limited monarchy, parliamentary monarchy or democratic monarchy, is a form of monarchy in which the monarch exercises their authority in accordance with a constitution and is not alone in making decisions.[1][2][3][4] Constitutional monarchies differ from absolute monarchies (in which a monarch is the only decision-maker) in that they are bound to exercise powers and authorities within limits prescribed by an established legal framework.

span.subject: Constitution
span.text: A constitution, or supreme law, is the aggregate of fundamental principles or established precedents that constitute the legal basis of a polity, organization or other type of entity, and commonly determines how that entity is to be governed.[1]

span.subject: Constitutional monarchy

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Compost is a mixture of ingredients used as plant fertilizer and to improve soil's physical, chemical, and biological properties.

references.label: P1.1
references.text: Compost is a mixture of ingredients used as plant fertilizer and to improve soil's physical, chemical, and biological properties.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: It is commonly prepared by decomposing plant and food waste, recycling organic materials, and manure.

references.label: P1.2
references.text: It is commonly prepared by decomposing plant and food waste, recycling organic materials, and manure.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: The resulting mixture is rich in plant nutrients and beneficial organisms, such as bacteria, protozoa, nematodes, and fungi.

references.label: P1.3
references.text: The resulting mixture is rich in plant nutrients and beneficial organisms, such as bacteria, protozoa, nematodes, and fungi.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Compost improves soil fertility in gardens, landscaping, horticulture, urban agriculture, and organic farming, reducing dependency on commercial chemical fertilizers.[1] The benefits of compost include providing nutrients to crops as fertilizer, acting as a soil conditioner, increasing the humus or humic acid contents of the soil, and introducing beneficial microbes that help to suppress pathogens in the soil and reduce soil-borne diseases.

references.label: P1.4
references.text: Compost improves soil fertility in gardens, landscaping, horticulture, urban agriculture, and organic farming, reducing dependency on commercial chemical fertilizers.[1] The benefits of compost include providing nutrients to crops as fertilizer, acting as a soil conditioner, increasing the humus or humic acid contents of the soil, and introducing beneficial microbes that help to suppress pathogens in the soil and reduce soil-borne diseases.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: At the most basic level, composting requires gathering a mix of green waste (nitrogen-rich materials such as leaves, grass, and food scraps) and brown waste (woody materials rich in carbon, such as stalks, paper, and wood chips).[1] The materials break down into humus in a process taking months.[2] Composting can be a multistep, closely monitored process with measured inputs of water, air, and carbon- and nitrogen-rich materials.

references.label: P2.1
references.text: At the most basic level, composting requires gathering a mix of green waste (nitrogen-rich materials such as leaves, grass, and food scraps) and brown waste (woody materials rich in carbon, such as stalks, paper, and wood chips).[1] The materials break down into humus in a process taking months.[2] Composting can be a multistep, closely monitored process with measured inputs of water, air, and carbon- and nitrogen-rich materials.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: The decomposition process is aided by shredding the plant matter, adding water, and ensuring proper aeration by regularly turning the mixture in a process using open piles or windrows.[1][3] Fungi, earthworms, and other detritivores further break up the organic material.

references.label: P2.2
references.text: The decomposition process is aided by shredding the plant matter, adding water, and ensuring proper aeration by regularly turning the mixture in a process using open piles or windrows.[1][3] Fungi, earthworms, and other detritivores further break up the organic material.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Aerobic bacteria and fungi manage the chemical process by converting the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide, and ammonium ions.

references.label: P2.3
references.text: Aerobic bacteria and fungi manage the chemical process by converting the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide, and ammonium ions.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Composting is an important part of waste management, since food and other compostable materials make up about 20% of waste in landfills, and due to anaerobic conditions, these materials take longer to biodegrade in the landfill.[4][5] Composting offers an environmentally superior alternative to using organic material for landfill because composting reduces methane emissions due to anaerobic conditions, and provides economic and environmental co-benefits.[6][7] For example, compost can also be used for land and stream reclamation, wetland construction, and landfill cover.

span.subject: Vermicompost
span.text: Vermicompost (vermi-compost) is the product of the decomposition process using various species of worms, usually red wigglers, white worms, and other earthworms, to create a mixture of decomposing vegetable or food waste, bedding materials, and vermicast.

span.subject: Vermicompost
span.text: This process is called vermicomposting, with the rearing of worms for this purpose is called vermiculture.

references.label: P4.2
references.text: This process is called vermicomposting, with the rearing of worms for this purpose is called vermiculture.

span.subject: Vermicompost
span.text: Vermicast (also called worm castings,[a] worm humus, worm poop, worm manure, or worm faeces) is the end-product of the breakdown of organic matter by earthworms.[1] These excreta have been shown to contain reduced levels of contaminants and a higher saturation of nutrients than the organic materials before vermicomposting.[2]

span.subject: Vermicompost
span.text: Vermicompost contains water-soluble nutrients which may be extracted as vermiwash and is an excellent, nutrient-rich organic fertilizer and soil conditioner.[3] It is used in gardening and sustainable, organic farming.

span.subject: Constitution
span.text: A constitution, or supreme law, is the aggregate of fundamental principles or established precedents that constitute the legal basis of a polity, organization or other type of entity, and commonly determines how that entity is to be governed.[1]

span.subject: Constitutional monarchy
span.text: Constitutional monarchy, also known as limited monarchy, parliamentary monarchy or democratic monarchy, is a form of monarchy in which the monarch exercises their authority in accordance with a constitution and is not alone in making decisions.[1][2][3][4] Constitutional monarchies differ from absolute monarchies (in which a monarch is the only decision-maker) in that they are bound to exercise powers and authorities within limits prescribed by an established legal framework.

span.subject: Fermentation
span.text: Fermentation is a type of anaerobic metabolism that harnesses the redox potential of the reactants to make adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and organic end products.[1][2] Organic molecules, such as glucose or other sugars, are catabolized and their electrons are transferred to other organic molecules (cofactors, coenzymes, etc.).[1] Anaerobic glycolysis is a related term used to describe the occurrence of fermentation in organisms (usually multicellular organisms such as animals) when aerobic respiration cannot keep up with the ATP demand, due to insufficient oxygen supply or anaerobic conditions.

span.subject: Pasteurization
span.text: In food processing, pasteurization (-isation) is a process of food preservation in which packaged foods (e.g., milk and fruit juices) are treated with mild heat, usually to less than 100 °C (212 °F), to eliminate pathogens and extend shelf life.

span.subject: Pasteurization
span.text: Pasteurization either destroys or deactivates microorganisms and enzymes that contribute to food spoilage or the risk of disease, including vegetative bacteria, but most bacterial spores survive the process.[1][2]

span.text: Pasteurization is named after French microbiologist Louis Pasteur, whose research in the 1860s demonstrated that thermal processing would deactivate unwanted microorganisms in wine.[3][4] Spoilage enzymes are also inactivated during pasteurization.

span.subject: Barcelona
span.text: With a population of 1.7 million within city limits,[3] its urban area extends to numerous neighbouring municipalities within the province of Barcelona and is home to around 5.7 million people,[4] making it the fifth most populous urban area of the European Union after Paris, the Ruhr area, Madrid, and Milan.[4] It is one of the largest metropolises on the Mediterranean Sea, located on the coast between the mouths of the rivers Llobregat and Besòs, and bounded to the west by the Serra de Collserola mountain range.

span.subject: Amateur astronomy
span.text: Amateur astronomy is a hobby where participants enjoy observing, studying, or imaging celestial objects in the sky using the unaided eye, binoculars, telescopes, and other gadgets.

span.subject: Amateur astronomy
span.text: Although scientific research may not be their primary goal, some amateur astronomers contribute to citizen science by monitoring variable stars,[1] double stars,[2] sunspots,[3] and occultations of stars by the Moon[4] or asteroids,[4] as well as by discovering transient astronomical events, such as comets,[5] galactic novae[6] or supernovae in other galaxies.[7]

span.text: The resulting mixture is rich in plant nutrients and beneficial organisms, such as bacteria, protozoa, nematodes, and fungi.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Compost improves soil fertility in gardens, landscaping, horticulture, urban agriculture, and organic farming, reducing dependency on commercial chemical fertilizers.[1] The benefits of compost include providing nutrients to crops as fertilizer, acting as a soil conditioner, increasing the humus or humic acid contents of the soil, and introducing beneficial microbes that help to suppress pathogens in the soil and reduce soil-borne diseases.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: At the most basic level, composting requires gathering a mix of green waste (nitrogen-rich materials such as leaves, grass, and food scraps) and brown waste (woody materials rich in carbon, such as stalks, paper, and wood chips).[1] The materials break down into humus in a process taking months.[2] Composting can be a multistep, closely monitored process with measured inputs of water, air, and carbon- and nitrogen-rich materials.

span.text: The decomposition process is aided by shredding the plant matter, adding water, and ensuring proper aeration by regularly turning the mixture in a process using open piles or windrows.[1][3] Fungi, earthworms, and other detritivores further break up the organic material.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Composting is an important part of waste management, since food and other compostable materials make up about 20% of waste in landfills, and due to anaerobic conditions, these materials take longer to biodegrade in the landfill.[4][5] Composting offers an environmentally superior alternative to using organic material for landfill because composting reduces methane emissions due to anaerobic conditions, and provides economic and environmental co-benefits.[6][7] For example, compost can also be used for land and stream reclamation, wetland construction, and landfill cover.

span.subject: Constitutional monarchy
span.text: Constitutional monarchy, also known as limited monarchy, parliamentary monarchy or democratic monarchy, is a form of monarchy in which the monarch exercises their authority in accordance with a constitution and is not alone in making decisions.[1][2][3][4] Constitutional monarchies differ from absolute monarchies (in which a monarch is the only decision-maker) in that they are bound to exercise powers and authorities within limits prescribed by an established legal framework.

span.text: A significant coastal urban area in the Mediterranean, Athens is also the capital of the Attica region and is the southernmost capital on the European mainland.

span.subject: Athens

span.subject: Athens
span.text: Athens is one of the world's oldest cities, with its recorded history spanning over 3,400 years,[10] and its earliest human presence beginning somewhere between the 11th and 7th millennia BC.

references.label: P5.1

span.subject: Athens
span.text: According to Greek mythology, the city was named after Athena, the ancient Greek goddess of wisdom, but modern scholars generally agree that the goddess took her name after the city.[11] Classical Athens was one of the most powerful city-states in ancient Greece.

references.label: P5.2

span.subject: Athens
span.text: It was a centre for Ancient Greek democracy, the arts, education and philosophy,[12][13] and was highly influential throughout the Hellenistic world and the European continent, particularly in ancient Rome.[14] For this reason it is often regarded as the cradle of Western civilisation and the birthplace of democracy in its own right independently from the rest of Greece.[15][16]

span.subject: Athens
span.text: In modern times Athens is a large cosmopolitan metropolis and central to economic, financial, industrial, maritime, political and cultural life in Greece.

span.subject: Athens
span.text: It is a Beta (+) – status global city according to the Globalization and World Cities Research Network,[17] and is one of the biggest economic centres in Southeast Europe.

span.subject: Athens

span.subject: Amateur astronomy
span.text: Amateur astronomy is a hobby where participants enjoy observing, studying, or imaging celestial objects in the sky using the unaided eye, binoculars, telescopes, and other gadgets.

span.subject: Amateur astronomy
span.text: Although scientific research may not be their primary goal, some amateur astronomers contribute to citizen science by monitoring variable stars,[1] double stars,[2] sunspots,[3] and occultations of stars by the Moon[4] or asteroids,[4] as well as by discovering transient astronomical events, such as comets,[5] galactic novae[6] or supernovae in other galaxies.[7]

span.subject: Apparent magnitude

span.text: Its value depends on its intrinsic luminosity, its distance, and any extinction of the object's light caused by interstellar dust or atmosphere along the line of sight to the observer.

span.text: The scale is reverse logarithmic: the brighter an object is, the lower its magnitude number.

span.subject: Apparent magnitude
span.text: A difference of 1.0 in magnitude corresponds to the brightness ratio of [TeX: {\displaystyle {\sqrt[{5}]{100}}}] , or about 2.512.

span.subject: Apparent magnitude
span.text: The brightest astronomical objects have negative apparent magnitudes, such as Venus at magnitude −4.2 or Sirius at magnitude −1.46.

span.subject: Apparent magnitude
span.text: The faintest stars visible with the naked eye on the darkest night have apparent magnitudes of about +6.5, though this varies depending on a person's eyesight, their altitude, and atmospheric conditions when viewing.[2] The apparent magnitude of known objects can range from −26.832 for our Sun to about +31.5 for objects in deep space imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope.[3]

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Compost is a mixture of ingredients used as plant fertilizer and to improve soil's physical, chemical, and biological properties.

references.label: P1.1
references.text: Compost is a mixture of ingredients used as plant fertilizer and to improve soil's physical, chemical, and biological properties.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: It is commonly prepared by decomposing plant and food waste, recycling organic materials, and manure.

references.label: P1.2
references.text: It is commonly prepared by decomposing plant and food waste, recycling organic materials, and manure.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: The resulting mixture is rich in plant nutrients and beneficial organisms, such as bacteria, protozoa, nematodes, and fungi.

references.label: P1.3
references.text: The resulting mixture is rich in plant nutrients and beneficial organisms, such as bacteria, protozoa, nematodes, and fungi.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Compost improves soil fertility in gardens, landscaping, horticulture, urban agriculture, and organic farming, reducing dependency on commercial chemical fertilizers.[1] The benefits of compost include providing nutrients to crops as fertilizer, acting as a soil conditioner, increasing the humus or humic acid contents of the soil, and introducing beneficial microbes that help to suppress pathogens in the soil and reduce soil-borne diseases.

references.label: P1.4
references.text: Compost improves soil fertility in gardens, landscaping, horticulture, urban agriculture, and organic farming, reducing dependency on commercial chemical fertilizers.[1] The benefits of compost include providing nutrients to crops as fertilizer, acting as a soil conditioner, increasing the humus or humic acid contents of the soil, and introducing beneficial microbes that help to suppress pathogens in the soil and reduce soil-borne diseases.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: At the most basic level, composting requires gathering a mix of green waste (nitrogen-rich materials such as leaves, grass, and food scraps) and brown waste (woody materials rich in carbon, such as stalks, paper, and wood chips).[1] The materials break down into humus in a process taking months.[2] Composting can be a multistep, closely monitored process with measured inputs of water, air, and carbon- and nitrogen-rich materials.

references.label: P2.1
references.text: At the most basic level, composting requires gathering a mix of green waste (nitrogen-rich materials such as leaves, grass, and food scraps) and brown waste (woody materials rich in carbon, such as stalks, paper, and wood chips).[1] The materials break down into humus in a process taking months.[2] Composting can be a multistep, closely monitored process with measured inputs of water, air, and carbon- and nitrogen-rich materials.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: The decomposition process is aided by shredding the plant matter, adding water, and ensuring proper aeration by regularly turning the mixture in a process using open piles or windrows.[1][3] Fungi, earthworms, and other detritivores further break up the organic material.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Aerobic bacteria and fungi manage the chemical process by converting the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide, and ammonium ions.

references.label: P2.3
references.text: Aerobic bacteria and fungi manage the chemical process by converting the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide, and ammonium ions.

span.subject: Compost
span.text: Composting is an important part of waste management, since food and other compostable materials make up about 20% of waste in landfills, and due to anaerobic conditions, these materials take longer to biodegrade in the landfill.[4][5] Composting offers an environmentally superior alternative to using organic material for landfill because composting reduces methane emissions due to anaerobic conditions, and provides economic and environmental co-benefits.[6][7] For example, compost can also be used for land and stream reclamation, wetland construction, and landfill cover.

span.subject: Vermicompost
span.text: Vermicompost (vermi-compost) is the product of the decomposition process using various species of worms, usually red wigglers, white worms, and other earthworms, to create a mixture of decomposing vegetable or food waste, bedding materials, and vermicast.

span.subject: Vermicompost
span.text: This process is called vermicomposting, with the rearing of worms for this purpose is called vermiculture.

references.label: P4.2
references.text: This process is called vermicomposting, with the rearing of worms for this purpose is called vermiculture.

span.subject: Vermicompost
span.text: Vermicast (also called worm castings,[a] worm humus, worm poop, worm manure, or worm faeces) is the end-product of the breakdown of organic matter by earthworms.[1] These excreta have been shown to contain reduced levels of contaminants and a higher saturation of nutrients than the organic materials before vermicomposting.[2]

span.subject: Vermicompost
span.text: Vermicompost contains water-soluble nutrients which may be extracted as vermiwash and is an excellent, nutrient-rich organic fertilizer and soil conditioner.[3] It is used in gardening and sustainable, organic farming.
